title: Anushirvan Pays for the Salt
text:
In his Gulistan, the Persian poet Saadi tells a story about Anushirvan the Just, the Sasanian king remembered in Persian tradition as the model of a fair ruler.

Anushirvan was out hunting, and his servants were roasting game for him at the hunting ground. They discovered that they had no salt. A servant was sent to a nearby village to fetch some. As he left, the king called after him to pay for the salt, so that it would not become a custom and the village be ruined.

His companions were puzzled. What harm could come from a pinch of salt? Anushirvan answered that oppression in the world had begun small. Everyone who came after added a little to it, until it reached its present size.

Saadi then adds his own verses to drive the point home. If the king eats a single apple from a peasant's orchard, his servants will pull up the tree by the roots. If the sultan allows five eggs to be taken by force, his soldiers will put a thousand chickens on the spit.
lesson: People below you copy what you allow yourself, and they copy it larger. Keep your own small habits clean, because they set the limit for everyone else.
people: Anushirvan the Just (Khosrow I), his servants
source: Saadi, Gulistan, Chapter 1 (On the Manners of Kings)
